clue.text: "As complete an —, as he that is known by wearing a clock of tuft-taffeta eighteen years" (Thomas Nashe, Lenten Stuffe)

definitions.text: "As complete an —, as he that is known by wearing a clock of tuft-taffeta eighteen years" (Thomas Nashe, Lenten Stuffe)

parts.words: "As complete an —, as he that is known by wearing a clock of tuft-taffeta eighteen years" (Thomas Nashe, Lenten Stuffe)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation: the missing word is Nashe's Spanish-derived term for a grand governor or pompous grandee

explanation.surface: A quotation from Nashe mocking a showy man who wore the same taffeta cloak for eighteen years.
explanation.walkthrough: The solver supplies the word missing from Nashe's sentence; 'clock' is the printed form of cloak.
explanation.definitionFit: Nashe uses the Spanish title for a provincial governor as a byword for a self-important dandy.

clue.text: Roguish start to a reviewed church history

indicators.note: the start of each of the four following words is taken in turn

explanation.surface: Someone opens a reviewed history of the church in a playful, roguish manner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'start to' applies to every word after it: A, R, C and H.
explanation.definitionFit: Arch describes a knowing, mischievous manner, a synonym of roguish.

clue.text: He paid dearly for his brother's lentil soup

definitions.text: He paid dearly for his brother's lentil soup

parts.words: He paid dearly for his brother's lentil soup
parts.note: the Genesis story of the elder twin who sold his birthright to his brother Jacob for a bowl of red lentil pottage

explanation.surface: A man overpays for his brother's cooking.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'price' was not money but his birthright, sold to Jacob in Genesis 25.
explanation.definitionFit: In Genesis the hungry elder twin traded his inheritance for Jacob's stew.

clue.text: PM and followers described by Powell

parts.note: p.m. stands for post meridiem, the part of the day after noon
men are the followers or subordinates of a leader

explanation.surface: A Prime Minister and his entourage are portrayed by someone called Powell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'PM' looks like Prime Minister; it is the time of day. Anthony Powell's 1931 novel supplies the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Anthony Powell wrote an early comic novel with this title about idle London bohemians.

clue.text: Irish one of Somerville and Ross produces some heat

definitions.text: Irish one of Somerville and Ross
definitions.meaning: Somerville and Ross wrote 'Some Experiences of an Irish R.M.', the resident magistrate
a unit of heat, 100,000 British thermal units, used in billing gas

explanation.surface: An Irish character from the Somerville and Ross stories generates warmth.
explanation.walkthrough: Split as THE RM, the Irish Resident Magistrate of the Somerville and Ross stories; run together it is the gas-bill unit.
explanation.definitionFit: The unit measures a quantity of heat energy, as on old British gas bills.

clue.text: Hopeless as Mowat's folk

definitions.meaning: without hope, in a dire state
Farley Mowat's 1959 book 'The ... People' is about the Ihalmiut of northern Canada

explanation.surface: Farley Mowat's people are described as beyond hope.
explanation.definitionFit: A desperate situation is one past hope; Mowat titled his book on starving Inuit people this way.

clue.text: — in water, like Keats

parts.note: Keats's ...-... epitaph reads 'Here lies one whose name was ... in water'

explanation.surface: Keats's name was set down in water, as his gravestone says.
explanation.definitionFit: The archaic participle meaning written completes Keats's Roman epitaph.

clue.text: Reportedly nightly location of Sapper's Dinner Club

definitions.text: Reportedly nightly location of Sapper's Dinner Club

parts.words: Reportedly nightly location of Sapper's Dinner Club
parts.note: 'nightly' said aloud is knightly: the place where King Arthur's knights sat, here also a dinner club's gathering board

explanation.surface: Where the members of Sapper's fictional Dinner Club meet every night.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reportedly' turns nightly into knightly, pointing to Arthur's knights; Sapper (H. C. McNeile) wrote 'The Dinner Club' stories.
explanation.definitionFit: Arthurian legend seats the knights at a circular board so none has precedence.

clue.text: Strong tourists?

definitions.meaning: L. A. G. Strong's 1945 novel '...' won the James Tait Black prize
tourists are people on journeys; the question mark admits they are only one kind

explanation.surface: Sturdy holidaymakers?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strong' looks like an adjective for the tourists; it is the novelist L. A. G. Strong.
explanation.definitionFit: Tourists are people who journey, and Strong gave his novel that plural title.

clue.text: Stendhal's Italian liqueur

definitions.meaning: Stendhal's novel 'La ... de Parme' is set in Italy, the charterhouse of Parma
a green or yellow herbal liqueur made by Carthusian monks

explanation.surface: The Italian drink that Stendhal favoured.
explanation.walkthrough: A Carthusian monastery gives both Stendhal's title and the monks' liqueur.
explanation.definitionFit: Carthusian monks distil the herbal spirit, named after their mother house; Stendhal used the word for a Parma monastery.

clue.text: Delacorta's moon goddess

definitions.meaning: the Roman goddess of the moon

explanation.surface: The moon goddess as Delacorta depicts her.
explanation.definitionFit: The Romans personified the moon as a goddess under this Latin name, also Delacorta's title.

clue.text: Openly declared believer of Bronte, Benson and Warner

definitions.meaning: one who professes a faith publicly
Charlotte Brontë, E. F. Benson and Rex Warner each wrote a novel of this title

explanation.surface: Brontë, Benson and Warner each wrote of a person who openly proclaims a creed.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who professes a belief openly is literally a professor of it, the title shared by three novels.

clue.text: Hardy soldier gets stranger hot in trick

indicators.note: the word 'in' signals that one group of letters sits inside the word for trick

parts.note: a dodge is a trick or ruse
rum means strange, so rummer means stranger
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on taps

explanation.surface: A tough soldier is caught out when something odder and hotter turns up in a ruse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hardy' looks like an adjective; it is Thomas Hardy, whose poem names the drummer boy buried on the veld.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Hardy's Boer War poem commemorates a young drummer buried in South Africa.

clue.text: Commentators, muddled as Holst (sic)

indicators.note: muddled tells us the letters of the next words are jumbled

explanation.surface: Critics confused, as Holst (sic) suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: Ancient scholars who wrote marginal notes explaining classical texts were annotators, a form of commentator.

clue.text: Appropriate words

parts.note: read appropriate as a verb, to take for one's own: taking someone else's words

explanation.surface: Fitting language.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Appropriate' reads as an adjective (suitable words); it is the verb, to steal them.
explanation.definitionFit: Passing off another writer's text as one's own is literary theft.

clue.text: Coo! a quill ingeniously used for seminars

indicators.note: using the letters ingeniously means rearranging them cleverly

explanation.surface: An exclamation as a quill pen is put to clever use for academic meetings.
explanation.definitionFit: Latin plural of a word for a formal academic conference or discussion meeting.

clue.text: Altruists, perhaps their opinions are extreme

indicators.note: perhaps signals the letters of the next word could be rearranged differently

explanation.surface: Unselfish people may hold extreme views.
explanation.definitionFit: Ultra- means beyond, so the word names people who take views to radical lengths.

clue.text: Haggard maiden

parts.note: H. Rider Haggard's novel '...-Maiden' about Roman Jerusalem; not a gaunt girl

explanation.surface: A worn-out young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Haggard' looks like gaunt; it is H. Rider Haggard.
explanation.definitionFit: Haggard titled his heroine after a gem, giving the word before maiden.

clue.text: It's instrumental, and Aristotle got on with it

definitions.meaning: a keyboard musical instrument, or any body part acting as a tool
Aristotle's logical works are called the Organon: this word followed by 'on'

explanation.surface: Something useful, and Aristotle managed to make progress with it.
explanation.walkthrough: Add ON to the answer and you get Organon, the name of Aristotle's logical treatises, meaning instrument.
explanation.definitionFit: A pipe or keyboard instrument, and literally 'tool' in Greek, the root of Aristotle's title.

clue.text: Clergyman's accessory identified by Herbert

definitions.meaning: the white band worn round a priest's neck
George Herbert's poem of this title, beginning 'I struck the board'

explanation.surface: Herbert recognises the item a priest wears.
explanation.definitionFit: A cleric wears a white neckband; George Herbert's rebellious poem uses it as a symbol of service.

clue.text: She was portrayed as a lady

definitions.text: She was portrayed as a lady

parts.words: She was portrayed as a lady
parts.note: Henry James's 'The Portrait of a Lady' has an American heroine as its subject

explanation.surface: A woman painted as a genteel lady.
explanation.walkthrough: 'portrayed as a lady' points to Henry James's novel title, The Portrait of a Lady.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry James's heroine is the subject of his novel's portrait.

clue.text: Secret police in attempt to reach Ekaterinburg

indicators.note: in tells us the answer lies inside the run of following words

explanation.surface: Bolshevik agents try to get to the city where the Tsar's family died.
explanation.definitionFit: The first Soviet state security organisation, set up in 1917, was a secret police force.

clue.text: Waugh hero, slippery type in secure closure

definitions.meaning: Basil, the cad of Evelyn Waugh's 'Black Mischief' and 'Put Out More Flags'
a tight fastening that nothing gets through

explanation.surface: Waugh's hero is a slippery character locked in safely.
explanation.definitionFit: Waugh's Basil bears the surname; it is also a marine mammal and an airtight closure.

clue.text: It was easy for Spenser

parts.note: an archaic word meaning easy, used by Edmund Spenser

explanation.surface: Spenser found it no trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'easy' is a definition, not a comment on Spenser's ease.
explanation.definitionFit: Old English word for easy, kept alive by Spenser's deliberately archaic verse.

clue.text: Its company offered by Jacobs

parts.note: W. W. Jacobs wrote the story collection '... Company'

explanation.surface: A firm's services supplied by someone called Jacobs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'company' looks like a firm; here it is a vessel's crew, in W. W. Jacobs's title.
explanation.definitionFit: A crew is a vessel's company, the title of Jacobs's book of sea stories.

clue.text: Revolutionary masses sent for evaluation

indicators.note: a revolution overturns things, so the letters of the next words are thrown into new order

explanation.surface: Rebellious crowds are sent away to be judged.
explanation.definitionFit: Judging the worth or quality of something is appraisal.

clue.text: Unwillingly introduce that of Pearl Buck

definitions.text: Unwillingly introduce that of Pearl Buck

parts.words: Unwillingly introduce that of Pearl Buck
parts.note: Drag on suggests bringing in reluctantly, and this word follows it

explanation.surface: Reluctantly bringing Pearl Buck into the conversation.
explanation.walkthrough: To drag something in is to introduce it unwillingly; 'drag on' plus the answer gives Buck's novel Dragon Seed.
explanation.definitionFit: Pearl Buck's wartime China novel ends in the word for a plant's germ.

clue.text: Possibly Saint-Exupéry's squadron

parts.note: Saint-Exupéry was a French aviator, so his unit would be a French air flight

explanation.surface: Perhaps the flying unit of the author of The Little Prince.
explanation.definitionFit: French word for a small air-force flight unit, the sort Saint-Exupéry flew with.
